topics.topic: Which Customer fields are removed or retained after customer erasure
questions: When a Customer is erased, do tax id, legal name, kind, restriction state and relationship-end state also disappear, or does any of them survive with the identity?
Does erasure also remove the customer's kind, tax id, legal name, restriction state and relationship-ended state, or do any of them survive?
Exactly which stored Customer facts are removed and which survive erasure, especially tax id, legal name, kind, restriction state, relationship-end date and revision?

judgement.why: This is the same question about Customer fields retained after erasure, and the relevant text has not changed.

precedent.topic: Customer fields removed or retained after erasure
quotes:
Erasing a customer's contact data (R0-06) is the end of its record: the
Customer keeps its identity and the fact that it was erased, and projects keep
naming it. There is no action that deletes a Customer whole.
precedent.why: Because the erased Customer keeps only its identity and erased fact, kind, tax id and legal name do not survive.

topics.topic: Which events advance the agent-session access version, including no-ops and refusals
questions: What does the session access version represent, and which of registration, grant, revoke, active-project change, pending-request replacement, request answer, archiving or project erasure advance it?
Which actions increment the access version, and do no-op or refused operations leave it unchanged?

When does the session access version change: registration, grant, revoke, active-project change or clear, request creation or replacement, request answer, project erasure, project archiving, and idempotent replays?

judgement.why: This repeats the previously judged question about the meaning and transition rules of the session access version.

precedent.topic: Meaning, concurrency role, and mutation rules of the agent-session access version
quotes: the session's granted project ids, its active project if any, whether it has a pending request, and the access version — no `personal_data` value (R0-32, R0-46, R0-64)
A change states the revision it was made against; a change against an older revision is refused and nothing changes. Every change is atomic.
precedent.why: Mutation preconditions, version-transition rules and stale-input behavior are rules and required tests owned by State 2.

topics.topic: Which primary actions must produce audit entries
questions: Exactly which primary actions produce audit entries—particularly room creation, artifact publication or withdrawal, session registration, pending-request changes, active-project changes, import and relationship end or resume?

Which exact primary actions create audit entries, especially room creation, artifact publication or withdrawal, session registration, active-project changes, access requests and answers, relationship changes, imports and archive replays?
Which exact primary actions produce audit entries?

judgement.why: This repeats the previously judged question about which actions and outcomes require audit entries.

precedent.topic: Actions and outcomes that require audit entries
quotes:
Registry records only significant changes of state: changes to projects and
customer records, granting and revoking an agent session's projects,
restricting processing and lifting it, and erasures and anonymisations. Ordinary reads, agent calls and the inner steps of flows
are not recorded in Registry; security events of the infrastructure are
handled by the infrastructure, outside Registry.

- **Audit.** A minimal log of significant changes of state (R0-58): time, the
  acting principal (owner, which service, agent through Kernel), the change,
  the project or customer, the outcome, the contract and release version, and
  a confirmation id where the owner confirmed.
precedent.why: The exact event-selection and outcome-recording criteria are operational rules and required tests owned by State 2.

topics.topic: Failure and no-op semantics for active-project changes and project revocation
questions: What observable failure is returned when the owner tries to change or revoke access for an unknown agent session?
What are the outcomes for an unknown session, an unknown project, setting the already-active project, clearing an already-empty active project, and revoking a granted project that is not active?

quotes: | change the active project or revoke a project | owner | the session's active project changes, or is cleared, which revokes nothing (R0-70); or the project leaves the session's set, and every later operation on it in that session — a running flow's next step included — is refused (R0-46) | a project not in the set answers that it is not granted; an archived project cannot be made active (R0-70) |

The owner may clear a session's active project, which revokes nothing. Making
an archived project active is refused, as granting one is; a project archived
while active stays active, and agent writes on it are refused (R0-12).
judgement.divergence: One implementation refuses an unknown session distinctly and returns unchanged for repeated active-project changes or clears; another treats the session as having no grant or accepts repeated operations as changes, which the owner notices in the returned failure or state.
judgement.why: The action names a session but omits its unknown-session failure, leaving an observable failure choice inside State 0 even though detailed no-op and version rules can later be settled in State 2.

topics.topic: How anonymisation handles identifying data in retained artifact pointer fields
questions: What must happen when retained pointer fields contain identifying or personal text: refuse anonymisation, remove or redact pointers, require an owner attestation, or accept that the result may not be anonymous?
What happens on anonymisation when a retained `uri`, `payload_ref` or digest may itself identify the customer or object?

judgement.why: This is the same question about identifying values in retained artifact pointers during anonymisation, and the governing passages have not changed.

precedent.topic: How anonymisation handles retained uninspected artifact pointer values
quotes: A project's technical identity, status and artifact pointers are kept only where it is shown that they no longer allow re-identification and a justified purpose for keeping them is recorded; `validate` then answers `archived`. Otherwise the record is deleted whole, and `validate` answers `not_found`.
Narrowed by R0-60: the owner chooses between the two when erasing; the showing and the purpose are recorded in the governance.
precedent.why: Retention is permitted only after a governance-recorded showing that the retained identity and pointers no longer allow re-identification; otherwise the project is deleted whole.

topics.topic: Relationship end-date ownership, validation, and repeated end or resume semantics
questions: Is the relationship-end date an owner-supplied effective date or Registry's current date, and what validation applies to it?
What happens on repeated end or resume, and may ending again replace the recorded end date?
Is the end date supplied by the owner or assigned by Registry, and what happens when ending an already-ended relationship or resuming one that is not ended?

quotes: | end or resume a customer relationship | owner | the Customer marked as ended on that date, or the mark cleared; archiving its projects does not end it (R0-49, R0-57, R0-60) | unknown or erased customer refused |

The end of a relationship with a customer is recorded by the owner, by an
explicit action; archiving the customer's projects does not end it.
Narrowed by R0-60: resuming clears the mark; Registry keeps no deletion date.
judgement.divergence: One implementation accepts an effective date supplied by the owner, while another records Registry's current date; the owner notices a different relationship-end date in Customer reads and retention review.
judgement.why: The action promises an end date without identifying whether it is an input or generated output, which is an unnamed input choice within State 0; repeated-transition rules may subsequently be defined in State 2.

topics.topic: Semantics and revision effects of repeated restriction or lift operations
questions: Are repeated restrict or lift operations no-ops, refusals, or accepted changes that advance the Customer revision?
Are repeated restriction and lift requests idempotent successes, or are invalid state transitions refused, and do successful no-ops move the customer revision?

quotes: | restrict or lift a restriction on a customer | owner | the Customer marked restricted, or no longer restricted where a lawful ground allows it; while restricted, its contact and fiscal data stay stored and reach no one but the owner (R0-80), no project may newly name it, and every other use of its contact data is refused — Registry admits no exception; where a lawful ground allows processing, the owner lifts the restriction (R0-65); corrections of its existing projects that do not use that data go on, and `context` keeps its `customer_ref` (R0-37, R0-51, R0-55) | unknown or erased customer refused |
judgement.why: Repeated-transition, no-op, refusal and revision-advancement semantics are rules and required tests owned by State 2.

topics.topic: Semantics of granting an already-granted project, including making it active
questions: Does granting an already granted project return unchanged, fail, or still advance the access version; and can the same call still make it active?
What happens when the owner grants an already-granted project, with or without asking to make it active?

quotes: | grant a project to an agent session | owner | the project joins the session's granted set; the owner may also make it the session's active project (R0-46) | unknown or archived project refused; unknown session refused |
judgement.why: The behavior of an idempotent repeated grant and its version effects is a mutation rule owned by State 2.

topics.topic: When billing data may be read and whether Registry enforces the permitted purpose
questions: May PresuPro call the billing-data read while rendering a draft or preview, or only as part of issuing a document; and is that purpose enforced by Registry or trusted to PresuPro?
May PresuPro read billing data while rendering drafts and previews, or only at the act of issuance, and can Registry enforce that condition?

quotes: | read a customer's billing data | a trusted service whose token allows it — today PresuPro, when it issues a document (R0-80) | the customer named by `customer_ref`: kind, tax id and legal name — for a person, the full name as on the identity document, which the owner records as its legal name — never its contact data, the ordinary name included; a fiscal value never recorded is marked absent, and the read is not refused for it (R0-83) | unknown customer refused; an erased or restricted customer refused (R0-65); any other caller refused |

A document is issued when it leaves the service to the customer — an invoice
issued, an estimate sent, a publication made; a draft, a preview or an unsent
version is not issued, keeps no personal value and reads it when rendered.
judgement.why: The primary action limits the read to document issuance, while R0-80 requires an unissued draft, preview or unsent version to read the values when rendered.

topics.topic: Whether project display names are classified as personal data throughout all contracts and rules
questions: Is a project's display name part of the `personal_data` class everywhere, including token authorization, output declarations and diagnostics rules?
Is the project display name part of the `personal_data` class everywhere, including the actor/trust-boundary definition and operation disclosure rules?

quotes:
A name such as "Reforma Pedreres
35" still carries a private object's address, which can identify a person, so
the display name is held as `personal_data`: it reaches the owner and a service
cleared for `personal_data` (R0-43), never the agent, and a consumer reads it
when it uses it instead of keeping it.
judgement.why: R0-82 explicitly classifies the project display name as `personal_data`; the earlier list of personal-data examples does not say it is exhaustive.

topics.topic: Whether refused or unsuccessful changes are recorded in the audit log
questions: Are refused or otherwise unsuccessful changes written to the audit log, and if so which ones?
Does the audit log contain refused attempts at significant changes, and if so which refusals?

judgement.why: This repeats the previously judged question about whether unsuccessful or refused outcomes are selected for audit recording.
